Adverse media screening: how banks review hits

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 28, 2026•8 min read

Adverse media screening is the search a bank or fintech runs on a customer, a beneficial owner or a counterparty for news and other public reports that link them to crime, terrorism, corruption or similar misconduct. It is also called negative news screening. The results feed the customer risk profile: a credible report can raise the risk rating, trigger more due diligence, prompt a review of the account activity or, in some cases, lead to an exit. US guidance treats it as a risk-based tool, and EU guidance names it as a reputation risk factor and an enhanced measure.

This guide explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What adverse media screening covers

An adverse media check is a point-in-time search, usually at onboarding or at a periodic review. Adverse media monitoring is the ongoing version: the customer's names stay in a watch list and new articles produce alerts. A program can use both and keep monitoring for the customers whose risk justifies it.

Sources range from national and local news to court and regulatory announcements and, for some customers, foreign-language outlets. The FATF's guidance on politically exposed persons (June 2013) notes that firms "frequently use the internet and media" to identify and verify PEPs, while warning that the information retrieved may not always be complete or reliable. The same caution is sensible for any adverse media search, so each hit needs a review before it changes anything.

What US guidance expects

The US customer due diligence rules do not require a media search for every customer. A footnote in the January 19, 2021 answers to frequently asked questions on suspicious activity reporting, issued by FinCEN with the Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA and OCC, says the customer due diligence regulations "do not categorically require the performance of media searches or particular screenings". The same footnote adds that a bank may decide, on the basis of risk, that a customer presents a higher risk and collect more information, "such as media searches".

The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual's customer due diligence section puts it the same way. A bank should set policies for deciding "whether and/or when, on the basis of risk", obtaining and reviewing more customer information, "for example through negative media search programs", would be appropriate. The manual also lists "Results of negative media search programs" among the events that can prompt a review of a customer relationship, next to changes in ownership and law enforcement inquiries such as subpoenas and 314(a) requests.

So the US position is that the bank decides who gets screened, how often and how deeply, writes that down, and follows it. The manual tells examiners to focus primarily on whether the bank has effective processes to develop customer risk profiles, so the written procedure and the evidence that staff followed it carry the weight.

What EU guidance expects

The EBA's ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/02, consolidated) are more explicit. Guideline 2 lists the reputation of the customer and its beneficial owner as a customer risk factor and asks whether there are "adverse media reports or other relevant sources of information" about them, such as allegations of criminality or terrorism. Firms should judge credibility "on the basis of the quality and independence of the source of the data and the persistence of reporting". The guideline also warns that "the absence of criminal convictions alone may not be sufficient to dismiss allegations of wrongdoing."

For high-risk relationships, paragraph 4.64 lists adverse media searches among the enhanced measures a firm may apply, alongside information about family members, close business partners and past and present business activities. The sectoral guideline for retail banks (paragraph 9.13) gives "open source or adverse media searches" as one way to build a more complete customer profile.

When to run an adverse media search

A written procedure should say which moments trigger a search and for which customers. One way to set it up, consistent with the guidance above:

MomentWho is searchedWhat the guidance says
OnboardingCustomers and beneficial owners your procedure assigns to search, for example higher-risk segmentsRisk-based; the FFIEC manual ties extra information to the customer risk profile
High-risk relationshipsCustomers rated high risk, for example because of PEP status or ownership concernsEBA paragraph 4.64 (other high-risk situations) lists adverse media searches as an enhanced measure
Periodic reviewEach customer due for a periodic KYC reviewFrequency is set by the bank; the FFIEC manual sets no fixed cycle
Event-drivenAny customer named in a new article, subpoena, 314(a) match or unusual activityThe FFIEC manual lists negative media results as a review trigger

The FFIEC manual also says ongoing monitoring "does not impose a categorical requirement that the bank must update customer information on a continuous or periodic basis". Continuous adverse media monitoring is a choice the bank makes for the customers who warrant it.

What counts as adverse

The procedure needs a written definition of adverse. One way to anchor the topic list is the FATF's "designated categories of offences" in the glossary to the FATF Recommendations, which include participation in an organized criminal group, terrorism and terrorist financing, trafficking in human beings, corruption and bribery, fraud, environmental crime, tax crimes, insider trading and market manipulation, among others. Add the topics your own risk assessment cares about, such as sanctions evasion or regulatory enforcement against the customer's business.

Write the list into the procedure with search terms for each topic and the languages to cover for customers abroad. A topic list also helps reviewers set aside articles that mention a customer without alleging anything, such as routine business news.

How to review an adverse media hit, step by step

A review procedure analysts can follow the same way every time:

  1. Confirm the article is about this customer. Compare the name with date of birth, location, occupation, employer or company role and photo where available. A name match alone proves little; record which identifiers matched and which ruled the article out. For example, an article about a person with the same name but a different birth year and home city can be cleared as a false positive, with both differences noted.
  2. Classify the allegation against your topic list. Note whether it is an allegation, a charge, a conviction, a civil action or a regulatory finding, and how old it is.
  3. Judge the source. Following the EBA criteria, look at the quality and independence of the outlet, whether the reporting persists and whether other reliable sources repeat the claim. A single blog post and a court record do not carry the same weight.
  4. Check whether it is new. The 2021 FAQs say that when several alerts stem from the same event, a bank "does not need to independently investigate each alert" and may consider "whether the alert contains new or different information". Link duplicates to the first review instead of reopening it.
  5. Assess what it means for the relationship. Compare the allegation with what you know about the customer's business, source of funds and expected activity. If it is material and relevant to the customer's risk, update the customer information and reassess the risk profile, as the FFIEC manual describes.
  6. Decide and route. Options are to clear the hit, re-rate the customer, apply more due diligence, refer the customer for an activity review in AML case management, or recommend an exit. The FFIEC manual says the procedure should indicate who is authorized to change a customer's risk profile.
  7. Record the decision in words a tester can follow without asking the analyst.

On step 6, the 2021 FAQs are clear that negative news "does not automatically require the filing of a SAR". It may lead the bank to review the customer's activity and related information, such as third parties transacting with the account, and the SAR decision then rests on that review. If a SAR is filed, the article can support the SAR narrative, but the narrative should still describe the activity that made it suspicious, not only the news.

Keeping adverse media monitoring useful

Ongoing monitoring can produce many alerts about the same few stories. The 2021 FAQs note that many institutions "maintain a process for managing a high volume of alerts generated by news". Practical controls include deduplicating alerts by story, tuning which topics alert for which risk tiers, and sampling cleared alerts for quality review.

Monitoring also has to reach the risk rating. In its consent order against Bank of America, N.A. (No. 2026-03, announced October 13, 2026), FinCEN described a dynamic risk rating model that was "designed to incorporate negative news" but missed one customer's own securities filing disclosing a Department of Justice money laundering investigation. The order covered much wider program failures, and FinCEN imposed a $1,200,000,000 penalty. The lesson for screening teams is narrower: test that what your sources find actually changes the customer record.

Screening names against official lists is a separate control with its own rules: see how to review a sanctions screening hit.

What the review record should hold

  • the search or alert, the date, the names and aliases searched and the sources covered;
  • each article reviewed, with its link or copy, publication date and outlet;
  • the identifiers that matched or ruled the article out;
  • the topic, the allegation type and the credibility judgment, with the reason;
  • the decision, any change to the risk rating or due diligence, and any referral or case reference;
  • the reviewer, any approver, and the time of each step.

Verkflo's PEP and adverse media use case runs this review as an agent: when ComplyAdvantage returns an adverse media hit, it compares the hit with the customer file, summarizes the articles and briefs a reviewer, who makes the decision.

Common questions

Is adverse media screening required for US banks?

Not for every customer. The 2021 interagency FAQs say the CDD rules do not categorically require media searches. The FFIEC manual expects a risk-based policy on when to use negative media search programs, so each bank decides which customers to screen, writes it down and acts on the results.

Do we have to file a SAR because of negative news?

No. Negative news on its own does not require a SAR. It can prompt a review of the customer's activity, and the SAR decision follows from that review.

Do we need to investigate every alert about the same story?

No. The 2021 FAQs say a bank may consider whether a repeat alert adds new or different information instead of investigating each one separately.

How is adverse media different from sanctions screening?

Sanctions screening matches names against official lists with legal consequences, such as blocking under OFAC rules. Adverse media is unstructured reporting that the bank weighs as a risk factor. A news story can make a customer higher risk without being a legal bar.
